name: Building Web APIs with Python
author: Recurse
subject: web
description: FastAPI (with Flask comparisons): routes, Pydantic validation, errors, dependencies, SQLAlchemy, auth, tests and deploys.

lesson.intro: Most Python developer jobs involve building or maintaining a web API. You will build one with FastAPI, with Flask comparisons: routing, Pydantic validation, status codes, dependencies, SQLAlchemy, authentication, testing, async work and production deploys.
objectives: Build FastAPI endpoints with path, query and body parameters validated by Pydantic
Return the right status codes and one consistent error shape
Use dependencies for sessions and auth, and store data with SQLAlchemy
Test an API's contract with TestClient and dependency overrides
Choose def or async def, and run an API in production

sections.title: From an HTTP request to a Python function
sections.key: A web framework routes each request to one of your functions and handles parsing, validation, serialization and errors, so you write only the business logic.
sections.body:
A phone app sends `POST /orders` with a JSON body. Some Python function must check the order, save it and answer `201 Created`. A **web framework** is the code in between:

[[visual]]

A server process accepts connections and calls the framework through one of two interfaces. **WSGI** is the classic synchronous one. **ASGI** is its async successor, which also supports websockets.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

`@app.get("/health")` registers the function in the app's routing table. `@app.post`, `@app.put` and `@app.delete` work the same way for other methods.

visual.title: What the framework does around your code

steps.label: Routing
steps.detail: Method plus path, such as `GET /books/42`, picks one of your functions

steps.label: Parsing
steps.detail: Path, query string, headers and JSON body become Python values

steps.label: Validation
steps.detail: Bad input gets a 4xx answer before your code runs

steps.label: Your function
steps.detail: The business rules: only this part is yours

steps.label: Serialization
steps.detail: Your return value becomes JSON with a status code and headers

steps.label: Errors
steps.detail: Exceptions become proper HTTP error responses

visual.title: What you will see in job postings
rows: Type hints drive parsing, validation and interactive docs at `/docs`
Batteries included: ORM, admin, auth, migrations
visual.caption: gunicorn is a process-managing WSGI server; uvicorn is an ASGI server.

sections.deeper:
A request has a method, a path with an optional query string, headers and an optional body; a response has a status code, headers and a body (How the Web Works covers HTTP itself).

FastAPI is built on Starlette and Pydantic. Flask leaves more choices to you: you read the request yourself and pick your own validation and database libraries. Django REST Framework adds API tools on top of Django.

The decorator is the registration pattern from Advanced Python: it records your function in a table and returns it unchanged.
sections.pitfall: Running the development server in production. `--reload` and Flask's debug mode watch files and can expose an interactive debugger; production uses workers behind a proxy.

activity.title: Build a tiny router
activity.prompt: This is what a framework's routing table does. In handle(), look up routes.get((method, path)). If it is missing, return 405 when some route has the same path (any(p == path for _, p in routes)), otherwise 404. Call the handler with body only for POST.

props.task: Print 200 {'status': 'ok'}, then 201 {'msg': 'hi'}, then 404 {'detail': 'Not Found'}, then 405 {'detail': 'Method Not Allowed'}.

check.question: Which interface and server pair does a FastAPI app use?
check.explanation: FastAPI is built on Starlette, an ASGI framework, and uvicorn is the usual ASGI server. Flask and Django are WSGI frameworks served by gunicorn or similar.

sections.title: Routes, path parameters and query parameters
sections.key: A path parameter identifies one resource and a query parameter filters a collection; FastAPI converts both from type hints and answers 422 when conversion fails.
sections.body:
`GET /books/42` and `GET /books?q=dune&limit=5` carry inputs in two places. A **path parameter** identifies one resource. **Query parameters** filter, search, sort or paginate a collection.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Routes match **in declaration order**. If `/users/{user_id}` comes before `/users/me`, a request for `/users/me` hits the first route with user_id "me" and fails with 422. Declare fixed paths first.

Flask writes `@app.get("/books/<int:book_id>")`, where a non-matching segment gives 404 rather than 422, and you read `request.args.get("q")` and validate it yourself.

visual.title: Declaring inputs in FastAPI
rows: Path parameter, converted to int; `/books/abc` gets 422
Optional query parameter (it has a default)

sections.deeper:
`Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10` is the newer spelling of the same validated query parameter, and it reads well when reused.

The design side (REST APIs in Practice): plural nouns for collections, ids in the path, filters and pagination in the query string, and never a verb such as `/getBook` in the URL.

An upper bound such as `le=100` is not only validation: without it, `?limit=1000000` could dump a whole table in one request.
sections.pitfall: Declaring `/users/{user_id}` before `/users/me`. The first matching route wins, so "me" is treated as a user id; put fixed paths first.

activity.title: Match paths like a framework
activity.prompt: Use `re.sub(r"\{(\w+)\}", r"(?P<\1>[^/]+)", pattern)` inside compile_route, so each {name} becomes a named group. Then try swapping the first two routes and watch /users/me turn into user_id 'me'.

check.question: A FastAPI route is declared as @app.get("/books/{book_id}") with book_id: int. What does GET /books/abc return?
choices: 422 with a JSON error saying book_id must be an integer
check.explanation: FastAPI validates the path parameter against its type before calling your function and returns 422 with details. A Flask <int:book_id> route would not match at all, giving 404.

sections.title: Request bodies and validation with Pydantic
sections.key: A Pydantic model describes a JSON body once; FastAPI parses and validates it, and answers 422 listing every problem before your function runs.
sections.body:
Every field a client sends is untrusted: missing, the wrong type, too long, negative. **Pydantic** lets you describe the data once, as a class that subclasses `BaseModel`. When an endpoint parameter is a model, FastAPI reads the JSON body into it.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Use **separate input and output models**. `UserCreate` carries a password; `UserOut` adds the server's id and must never include the password hash. `response_model=UserOut` (or the return type) filters the response to exactly those fields.

`model_dump()` turns a model into a dict and `Model.model_validate(data)` builds one, so you can validate files and queue messages too.

visual.title: What a model checks
rows: Other models and `list[Model]` validate whole documents
One 422 lists them all, each with a location such as `["body", "title"]`, a type and a message

sections.code:
class BookIn(BaseModel):  # what clients send
    title: str = Field(min_length=1,
                       max_length=200)
    author: str
    year: int = Field(ge=1450)
    tags: list[str] = []

    @field_validator("tags")
    @classmethod
    def clean(cls, v):
        return [t.strip().lower() for t in v]

class BookOut(BookIn):  # what the API returns
    id: int

@app.post("/books", status_code=201,
          response_model=BookOut)
def create_book(book: BookIn):  # JSON body
    new = BookOut(id=len(BOOKS) + 1,
                  **book.model_dump())
    BOOKS[new.id] = new
    return new

client.post("/books", json={
    "title": "Dune", "author": "Herbert",
    "year": "1965", "tags": [" SciFi "]})
# 201 {'title': 'Dune', 'author': 'Herbert',
#  'year': 1965, 'tags': ['scifi'], 'id': 1}

client.post("/books", json={
    "title": "", "year": "soon"})
# 422, errors at title (string_too_short),
# author (missing) and year (int_parsing)
sections.deeper:
Pydantic's default "lax" mode converts obvious cases, such as the string "1965" to the int 1965. Strict mode (`Field(strict=True)` or a model config) rejects the string too.

A mutable default such as `tags: list[str] = []` is safe in a Pydantic model, because Pydantic copies defaults for each instance, unlike a plain function default.

In Flask you call validation yourself: `BookIn.model_validate(request.get_json())` inside `try/except ValidationError`, or use an extension that wires it up.
sections.pitfall: Returning a database object or dict straight from an endpoint without a response model. Every field goes out, including `password_hash` or internal flags; declare an output model.

activity.title: Validate like Pydantic, by hand
activity.prompt: Collect every problem instead of stopping at the first. Read fields with data.get(), convert year with int() inside try/except, check the ranges, and return (None, errors) if the list is not empty.

props.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Book:
    title: str
    year: int

def validate_book(data):
    """Return (Book, []) for valid data, or (None, errors) listing EVERY problem."""
    errors = []
    # title: required ("title: required"), a non-empty string ("title: must not be empty")
    # year: required ("year: required"), an int or digit string ("year: not an integer"),
    #       from 1450 to 2100 ("year: out of range")
    return Book(data.get("title"), data.get("year")), errors

for data in [{"title": "Dune", "year": "1965"}, {"title": "", "year": 3000}, {"year": "soon"}]:
    print(validate_book(data))
props.task: Print (Book(title='Dune', year=1965), []), then (None, ['title: must not be empty', 'year: out of range']), then (None, ['title: required', 'year: not an integer']).
props.expectOutput:
(Book(title='Dune', year=1965), [])
(None, ['title: must not be empty', 'year: out of range'])
(None, ['title: required', 'year: not an integer'])

check.question: A client POSTs {"title": "", "year": "soon"} to the create_book endpoint above. What happens?
choices: The book is saved with an empty title
FastAPI returns 500 because the year cannot be converted
Only the first error is returned
FastAPI returns 422 listing every problem, and create_book never runs
check.explanation: Pydantic validates the whole body and reports all errors together: title too short, author missing and year not an integer. Your function is called only with valid data.

sections.title: Status codes, errors and consistent responses
sections.key: Status codes are part of the API contract: pick them deliberately, keep one error shape, and map domain exceptions to HTTP in one place.
sections.body:
A mobile app gets `200 OK` with `{"error": "not found"}` and shows an empty screen, because its HTTP client only checks the status code.

[[visual]]

`raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Book not found")` stops the handler and sends `{"detail": "Book not found"}`. FastAPI's own errors use `detail` too, so every error has one shape.

Keep HTTP out of business logic. Stock checks raise **domain exceptions** such as `OutOfStock`, and one `@app.exception_handler` maps each to a status and body:

[[code]]

Unhandled exceptions become a generic 500, with the traceback in your logs. Never send stack traces to clients: they reveal paths, SQL and code structure to attackers.

visual.title: Status codes a CRUD API uses daily
rows: Success with nothing to return, such as a DELETE
Well-formed JSON that fails validation (FastAPI's default)
Not authenticated: missing or invalid credentials
Does not exist, or is hidden from this caller
Duplicate email, or a state clash
Our bug. Never sent on purpose for a client mistake

sections.deeper:
Why domain exceptions: the stock and payment code stays free of HTTP, so it can be reused from a CLI or a queue worker and tested without a web framework, and the HTTP mapping lives in one place instead of try/except blocks in every route.

401 versus 403 trips people up: 401 means "we do not know who you are", 403 means "we know, and the answer is no". Returning 404 instead of 403 is a deliberate choice when even confirming that a resource exists would leak information.

Flask's equivalents are `abort(404)` and `@app.errorhandler(OutOfStock)`.
sections.pitfall: Returning 200 with `{"error": ...}` in the body. Clients, monitoring and caches all read the status code; use a 4xx or 5xx so failures look like failures.

activity.title: Trigger each error on purpose
activity.prompt: This mock API stores tasks. Send requests that produce 400, 404, 405 and 415 responses and read each error body. The codes mean the same in every API, including the ones you build with FastAPI.

check.question: A logged-in user requests DELETE /teams/7, but they are not a member of team 7. Which status fits best?
choices: 403 Forbidden (or 404 if you hide that the team exists)
check.explanation: The user is authenticated, so 401 is wrong; they are simply not allowed. Many APIs return 404 instead so outsiders cannot even confirm the team exists.

sections.title: Dependency injection with Depends
sections.key: An endpoint declares what it needs with `Depends`, and FastAPI builds it per request: sessions, the current user, shared parameters, all swappable in tests.
sections.body:
Almost every endpoint needs the same things: a database session, the current user, settings. Building them inside each function repeats code and blocks testing. With **dependency injection**, the endpoint declares what it needs and the framework provides it.

`Annotated[Database, Depends(get_db)]` makes FastAPI call `get_db` per request and pass in the result. Dependencies can take headers, query parameters and other dependencies. Within one request each runs **once**, even if several ask for it.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

In tests, `app.dependency_overrides[get_current_user] = lambda: "test-user"` swaps a dependency everywhere, without patching imports.

visual.title: Good jobs for a dependency
rows: `get_db` **yields** a session; code after `yield` closes it after the response, even if the endpoint raised
`get_current_user` reads a token, raises 401 or returns the user. Listing it protects the endpoint

sections.deeper:
Dependencies form a graph that FastAPI resolves per request. Because results are cached within the request, two dependencies that both need `get_db` share the same session and transaction; `Depends(get_db, use_cache=False)` would force a second call.

Aliases such as `User = Annotated[str, Depends(get_current_user)]` keep signatures short and consistent across a codebase.

Flask has no built-in equivalent: apps keep per-request objects on `flask.g`, open and close sessions in `before_request` and `teardown_appcontext` hooks, and protect routes with decorators such as Flask-Login's `@login_required`.
sections.pitfall: Creating one database connection at import time and sharing it across requests. Concurrent requests interleave transactions on it; hand out a session per request through a yield dependency.

check.question: What runs the code after the yield in a dependency such as get_db?
choices: The client, when it closes the connection
Nothing: code after yield is ignored
FastAPI, after the response has been produced, even if the endpoint raised
check.explanation: FastAPI treats a yield dependency like a context manager: setup before the yield, cleanup after the request is handled. Wrapping the yield in try/finally guarantees the cleanup on errors too.

sections.title: A database layer with SQLAlchemy
sections.key: SQLAlchemy maps tables to classes; give each request its own Session, bind every value as a parameter, and change schemas through Alembic migrations.
sections.body:
API data must outlive the process: SQLite while learning, PostgreSQL in most production Python shops. You reach it two ways:

[[visual]]

In SQLAlchemy 2.0, models subclass `DeclarativeBase`. An **engine** holds the connection pool for one database URL, taken from configuration. A **Session** is a unit of work: `add` objects, query with `select(...)`, then `commit()` in one transaction or `rollback()`. A web app opens **one session per request** through a yield dependency.

[[code]]

Beware **lazy loading**: touching `book.author` for 50 books fires 50 extra queries, the **N+1 problem**. Load related rows up front with `options(selectinload(Book.author))`.

[[visual 2]]

items.title: A driver and raw SQL
points: You write the SQL
Values always bound as parameters: `WHERE title = ?` with a tuple
You map rows to objects yourself

items.title: An ORM
points: Tables become classes, rows become objects
The standard outside Django, which has its own ORM
Generates parameterized SQL for you

visual.caption: Never build SQL with f-strings: that is how SQL injection happens.

steps.label: Review and edit the generated script
Commit it with the code change

sections.code:
class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class Author(Base):
    __tablename__ = "authors"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(100))
    books: Mapped[list["Book"]] = (
        relationship(back_populates="author"))

class Book(Base):
    __tablename__ = "books"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(
        String(200))
    author_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(
        ForeignKey("authors.id"))
    author: Mapped[Author] = relationship(
        back_populates="books")

# in a real app the URL comes from config
engine = create_engine("sqlite:///:memory:")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)  # demo

with Session(engine) as session:
    fh = Author(name="Frank Herbert")
    session.add(Book(title="Dune", author=fh))
    session.commit()
    stmt = select(Book).options(
        selectinload(Book.author))
    for b in session.scalars(stmt):
        print(b.title, "by", b.author.name)
# Dune by Frank Herbert
sections.deeper:
Real projects never call `create_all` against production: Alembic compares models with the database and records each change as a reviewed, versioned script.

While developing, `create_engine(url, echo=True)` prints every SQL statement, which is how you spot an N+1 loop.

You will also meet **SQLModel**, which merges SQLAlchemy and Pydantic models into one class, and async engines (`create_async_engine` with asyncpg) for async endpoints. The raw-driver version of a lookup is `conn.execute("SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE title = ?", (title,))`.
sections.pitfall: Building SQL with f-strings, even inside an ORM's `text()` call. Bind every value as a parameter; the driver sends it as data, so it can never become SQL.

check.question: Why does a web app usually create one SQLAlchemy Session per request instead of one for the whole app?
choices: Sessions can only run one query each
Each request gets its own unit of work and transaction, so concurrent requests cannot mix their changes
A global session is slower to import
check.explanation: A Session tracks pending changes and an open transaction. Sharing one between concurrent requests interleaves their work; a session per request, closed afterwards, keeps them isolated while the engine's pool reuses connections.

sections.title: Authentication and authorization basics
sections.key: Authentication asks who is calling; authorization asks whether they may touch this resource. Check ownership on every object, not just that someone logged in.
sections.body:
Getting **authentication** wrong lets strangers in. Getting **authorization** wrong lets one customer read another's orders: **broken object level authorization** (an IDOR), the most common serious API flaw on OWASP's list.

[[visual]]

After login, the client sends a token on every request: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

[[visual 2]]

In FastAPI, `OAuth2PasswordBearer` reads the bearer token and a `current_user` dependency turns it into a user or raises **401**. Authorization raises **403**: by role, and by ownership.

[[code]]

visual.title: Passwords and secrets
rows: Store only slow, salted hashes: argon2, bcrypt or scrypt
A stolen table cannot be reversed quickly
`==` stops at the first difference, so timing leaks how much of a guess was right
Same error for a wrong username and a wrong password
Does not reveal which accounts exist

items.title: Opaque session token
points: Random string: `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`
The server looks it up in a database or cache
Easy to revoke: delete the row

items.title: Signed token (JWT)
points: Carries claims: user id (`sub`), role, expiry (`exp`)
The signature stops undetected changes; any server verifies it without a lookup
Valid until it expires: keep lifetimes short
Payload is only base64: anyone can read it

sections.deeper:
Never store passwords themselves. Libraries such as argon2-cffi, pwdlib or bcrypt are the usual choice; the standard library's `hashlib.scrypt` above is also a proper slow hash, and each user gets a unique random salt.

Because a JWT stays valid until it expires, pair short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens. Never put secrets in the payload.

A login form endpoint uses `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm`, which needs the python-multipart package. Browser apps often use cookie sessions instead of bearer tokens, which brings CSRF protection into play, and larger systems delegate login to an identity provider with OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.
sections.pitfall: Checking that a user is logged in but not that they own the resource. `GET /orders/1043` must verify `order.user_id` matches the caller, or anyone can read any order.

activity.title: Verify a signed token
activity.prompt: This is how a JWT's signature works, with the standard library. In verify(), recompute the HMAC of body exactly as sign() does, return None unless hmac.compare_digest(expected, sig) is true, then decode the payload and return None if it has expired.

props.task: Print {'sub': 'ana', 'role': 'member', 'exp': 1000}, then None for the forged token, then None for the expired one.

check.question: Bo is logged in and calls GET /orders/77, which belongs to Ana. The endpoint only checks that a valid token was sent. What is this bug called?
check.explanation: Authentication worked, but nobody checked that order 77 belongs to Bo. Every endpoint that loads a resource by id must compare its owner with the current user (or return 404).

sections.title: Testing an API with pytest and TestClient
sections.key: TestClient runs requests through the whole app in-process; test status and body for each case, and clear dependency overrides after every test.
sections.body:
An API's contract is its URLs, status codes and JSON shapes, so the most valuable tests send a request and check the response. **TestClient** does it in-process, with no server or network: routing, validation, dependencies, your code and serialization all run.

[[visual]]

Keep tests independent. A fixture gives each test fresh state through `app.dependency_overrides`, and clears the overrides after its `yield`, or they leak into later tests.

[[code]]

Test database code against the same database as production, such as a PostgreSQL container in CI, rolling back each test. SQLite hides differences in types, constraints and locking.

visual.title: What to cover for each endpoint
rows: Status **and** body: 201 and the created object
Missing field, wrong type, out of range: each 422
Unknown id: 404 with the expected error body
No token 401, wrong role 403, and no access to another user's resources
Empty lists, pagination limits, duplicates giving 409

sections.code:
@pytest.fixture
def client():
    repo = BookRepo()  # fresh per test
    over = app.dependency_overrides
    over[get_repo] = lambda: repo
    over[get_current_user] = lambda: "test"
    with TestClient(app) as c:
        yield c
    over.clear()  # no leaks into later tests

DUNE = {"title": "Dune", "year": 1965}

def test_create_then_fetch(client):
    r = client.post("/books", json=DUNE)
    assert r.status_code == 201
    book = r.json()
    got = client.get(f"/books/{book['id']}")
    assert got.json() == book

def test_missing_book_is_404(client):
    r = client.get("/books/999")
    assert r.status_code == 404
    assert r.json() == {"detail": "Not found"}

def test_writes_need_a_token(client):
    over = app.dependency_overrides
    del over[get_current_user]  # real check
    r = client.post("/books", json=DUNE)
    assert r.status_code == 401
sections.deeper:
Use parametrize for validation cases: one test body, a list of bad payloads (`{}`, an empty title, `"year": "soon"`), each expecting 422.

For a real database in CI, run a PostgreSQL service container (or the testcontainers library), apply migrations once, and wrap each test in a transaction that is rolled back.

Flask's built-in equivalent is `app.test_client()`. For async code paths, httpx's `AsyncClient` with an ASGI transport plus an async pytest plugin sends requests from async tests. Remember the test pyramid: most tests can still be fast unit tests of plain functions, with API tests checking wiring and contract.
sections.pitfall: Checking only the status code. A 200 with the wrong body, a missing field or another user's data still passes; assert on the JSON your clients depend on.

check.question: Why does the client fixture call app.dependency_overrides.clear() after its yield?
choices: So overrides from one test cannot leak into later tests that expect the real dependencies
To make the tests run faster
check.explanation: dependency_overrides lives on the shared app object. Without cleanup, a test that relies on the real auth check could silently run with the fake user from an earlier test.

sections.title: Sync or async endpoints, and background work
sections.key: Plain `def` endpoints run in a thread pool and may block; `async def` endpoints share the event loop, so one blocking call inside them stalls every request.
sections.body:
FastAPI accepts both `def` and `async def` endpoints, and picking wrong is one of the most common FastAPI performance bugs.

[[visual]]

Use `async def` only when everything slow inside is awaited with an async library, such as `httpx.AsyncClient` or asyncpg. With blocking libraries, use plain `def`, or wrap the call in `await asyncio.to_thread(fn)`. Dependencies follow the same rule.

[[code]]

Work the client should not wait for, such as emails, reports and video, leaves the request:

[[visual 2]]

items.title: `def`
points: Runs in a **thread pool**
A blocking call (`requests.get`, `time.sleep`, sqlite3, psycopg, a sync SQLAlchemy session) ties up one thread
The safe default

items.title: `async def`
points: Runs on the **event loop**
Each `await` lets the loop serve others: thousands of slow network calls per worker
One blocking call freezes **every** request on that worker

visual.title: Work that should not delay the response

items.title: `BackgroundTasks`
items.sub: small jobs, such as a welcome email
points: Runs after the response, in the web process
No extra infrastructure
Lost if the process dies, and no retries

items.title: A task queue
points: For slow, important or retryable work: PDF reports, bulk emails, video transcoding
The endpoint queues a job on Redis or RabbitMQ and returns 202 Accepted
Separate workers run it, with retries

sections.deeper:
CPU-heavy work (reports, image processing, machine learning inference) belongs in workers or separate services, never on the event loop: even `to_thread` only helps with waiting, not with Python computation, because of the GIL.

The queue-and-workers pattern from system design gives you persistence (jobs survive restarts), retries and independent scaling of workers.

Flask is synchronous: each request occupies a worker thread or process, which suits blocking libraries. Flask can run `async def` views, but each request still holds its worker, so it does not bring FastAPI-style concurrency (Quart is the async variant of Flask).
sections.pitfall: Calling a blocking library inside `async def`. `requests.get` or `time.sleep` there stalls every request on the worker; use an async client, plain `def`, or `asyncio.to_thread`.

check.question: An endpoint calls requests.get(url, timeout=10) (a blocking library). How should it be declared?
choices: It cannot be used in FastAPI at all
async def, so it is faster
Plain def, so FastAPI runs it in a thread pool
async def with time.sleep(0) before the call
check.explanation: Blocking code belongs in a plain def endpoint, which FastAPI runs in a worker thread. In an async def endpoint it would block the event loop for up to 10 seconds.

sections.title: Running and deploying a Python API
sections.key: In production, run several worker processes behind a proxy that terminates HTTPS, keep state outside the process, and run migrations before new code takes traffic.
sections.body:
`uvicorn main:app --reload` is perfect on a laptop: it restarts on every save and listens only on localhost. Production changes several things:

[[visual]]

Each worker has its own memory, so a module-level cache exists once per worker and can disagree between requests. Keep sessions, caches and uploads in a database, Redis or object storage.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Laptop to production
rows: Several **workers**, about one per core: `uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4` or `fastapi run --workers 4`. Flask and Django run under gunicorn
A reverse proxy or load balancer terminates HTTPS and spreads traffic. Set uvicorn's `--forwarded-allow-ips` so it trusts the proxy's headers
Settings and secrets from environment variables
Structured logs to stdout, a cheap `GET /health` for load balancers, request rates, errors and latency
A Docker image: slim base, dependencies in their own cached layer, a non-root user

steps.label: CI runs the tests on the merged commit
Build and push the Docker image
Run the database migrations
steps.detail: `alembic upgrade head`, compatible with the old code still running

steps.label: Roll out the new containers gradually
Watch health checks, error rates and latency

sections.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
# dependencies first: this layer stays
# cached while only the code changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir \
    -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
# never run as root
RUN useradd --create-home appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", \
     "--host", "0.0.0.0", \
     "--port", "8000", "--workers", "2"]
sections.deeper:
On Kubernetes or a container platform, teams often run one worker per container and let the platform run more containers. Flask apps start with something like `gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 "app:create_app()"`.

uvicorn trusts `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` only from addresses in `--forwarded-allow-ips` (localhost by default); set it to the proxy so the app sees the real client address and scheme.

Where it runs: a platform as a service (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku) for side projects; Google Cloud Run, AWS App Runner or ECS, Azure Container Apps or Kubernetes at work.
sections.pitfall: Keeping per-user state in a module-level dict or on local disk. With several workers, the next request may land on another process; use a database, Redis or object storage.

check.question: An API runs with --workers 4. A module-level dict caches recent results. What is true?
choices: Each worker process has its own copy, so the cache is not shared and can disagree between requests
Only the first worker can write to it
All four workers share the dict
check.explanation: Workers are separate processes with separate memory. Shared state belongs in an external store such as Redis or the database.

keyTerms.definition: The asynchronous interface between Python web servers and frameworks, used by FastAPI and Starlette and served by uvicorn.
The classic synchronous interface between Python web servers and frameworks, used by Flask and Django and served by gunicorn.
A value taken from a URL segment, such as 42 in /books/42, usually identifying one resource.
A key=value pair after ? in a URL, used to filter, search, sort or paginate a collection.
A class subclassing BaseModel whose type hints and Field constraints parse and validate data, such as a JSON body.
The status FastAPI returns when a request is well-formed but fails validation, listing every error.
A FastAPI route setting that filters and validates the response against a model, so extra fields cannot leak.
Declaring what an endpoint needs with Depends, so the framework provides it per request and tests can override it.
An object-relational mapper, such as SQLAlchemy, that maps database tables to classes and rows to objects.
A unit of work that tracks loaded and new objects and commits or rolls back their changes in one transaction.
A versioned script, such as one generated by Alembic, that changes a database schema in a repeatable way.
A credential sent in the Authorization: Bearer header that proves who the caller is.
A JSON Web Token: base64-encoded claims plus a signature, verifiable without a database lookup but readable by anyone.
FastAPI's in-process client that sends requests through the whole app in tests without starting a server.
A broker plus worker processes (Celery, RQ) that run slow or retryable jobs outside the request.
One of several copies of the app run by the server to use multiple CPU cores; each has its own memory.

summary: A framework routes requests and handles parsing, validation, JSON and errors; FastAPI is ASGI on uvicorn, Flask is WSGI.
Path parameters identify, query parameters filter, Pydantic validates bodies with 422.
Pick status codes on purpose and map domain errors to HTTP in one place.
Depends supplies sessions and users per request; overrides fake them in tests.
One Session per request, bound parameters, Alembic migrations; check ownership on every resource.
def for blocking code, async def only with async libraries; several workers in production.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who knows basic Python what happens, step by step, between a phone app sending POST /books with a JSON body and FastAPI sending back 201 Created, including where validation, dependencies and the database come in.

questions.question: Which job is NOT something a web framework like FastAPI or Flask does for you?
choices: Turning an HTTPException into a 404 response
Converting a returned dict into a JSON response
Deciding which business rules an order must satisfy
questions.explanation: Routing, parsing, serialization and error responses are framework plumbing. The business rules are your code, which is why keeping them in plain functions makes them easy to test.

questions.question: Match each framework or server with its description.

pairs.right: ASGI framework where type hints drive parsing, validation and docs
Small, explicit WSGI framework with many extensions
Batteries-included framework with ORM, admin and auth
ASGI server that runs FastAPI apps
Process-managing WSGI server often used for Flask and Django

questions.explanation: Frameworks shape how you write handlers; servers accept connections and call the framework. FastAPI plus uvicorn and Flask plus gunicorn are the common pairs.

questions.question: What path does FastAPI serve its interactive, auto-generated API documentation on by default?
questions.explanation: FastAPI builds an OpenAPI schema from your routes and models (at /openapi.json) and serves Swagger UI at /docs and ReDoc at /redoc.

questions.question: Complete the decorator so this function handles DELETE requests to /books/{book_id}.
questions.explanation: FastAPI (and Flask 2.0 and later) has one decorator per HTTP method: get, post, put, patch and delete. A DELETE request to a path registered only with get would receive 405 Method Not Allowed.

questions.question: You need an endpoint that searches books by title and returns at most 20 results. How should the inputs arrive?
choices: GET /books with the search term in a header
questions.explanation: Search terms, filters and page sizes modify a request for the books collection, so they belong in the query string. Path segments identify specific resources.

questions.question: Complete the signature so page is an optional query parameter that defaults to 1 and must be at least 1.
questions.explanation: Query declares a query-string parameter with a default and constraints, so ?page=0 is rejected with 422. Path is for path segments and Body for JSON bodies.

questions.question: GET /users/me returns 422: user_id should be a valid integer. Why?
choices: me is a reserved word in FastAPI
Routes match in declaration order, so /users/me hits /users/{user_id} first; declare /users/me before it
FastAPI does not allow two routes under /users
questions.explanation: The parameterized route was declared first and matches any single segment, including "me", which then fails int conversion. Fixed paths must come before parameterized ones.

questions.question: In FastAPI, def list_books(q: str | None = None, limit: int = 10). Which request is rejected?
questions.explanation: limit is declared as an int, and "five" cannot be converted, so FastAPI answers 422. Both parameters have defaults, so leaving either out is fine.

questions.question: Why have both a UserCreate and a UserOut model instead of one User model?
choices: It makes responses faster to serialize
Pydantic cannot reuse a model twice
Input needs fields such as password that must never be returned, and output has server fields such as id
FastAPI requires every endpoint to have two models
questions.explanation: Separate models make the contract explicit in both directions. response_model=UserOut filters the response, so a password hash can never slip out even if the object you return has one.

questions.question: What status code does FastAPI return when a request body fails Pydantic validation?
questions.explanation: 422 Unprocessable Entity: the JSON parsed fine, but its content broke the rules. The body lists each error with its location, type and message.

questions.question: With year: int in a Pydantic model (default settings), which JSON values for year are accepted? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: By default Pydantic converts a numeric string such as "1965" to an int. A float with a fractional part, text and null are rejected for a required int. Strict mode would also reject the string.

questions.question: Complete the model so name must be between 2 and 50 characters long.
questions.explanation: Field adds constraints to a model field; for strings they are min_length and max_length. Query is for query parameters, not body fields.

questions.question: Match each situation with the status code an API should return.

pairs.left: Signup with an email that is already registered
Request without any credentials to a protected endpoint
An unhandled exception in your code

questions.explanation: The status code is the first thing clients and monitoring read. 409 signals a conflict with existing state, and 500 should only ever appear for your own bugs.

questions.question: Why raise a domain exception such as OutOfStock in business code and map it with @app.exception_handler, instead of raising HTTPException there?
choices: FastAPI forbids HTTPException outside route functions
Business code stays free of HTTP, so it can be reused and tested without a web framework, and the mapping lives in one place
questions.explanation: The same stock logic might run from a CLI, a queue worker or a test. HTTPException belongs at the web edge; domain errors are translated to HTTP there, once.

questions.question: Clients report that failed lookups look like successes in their dashboards. What is wrong?
choices: It returns 200 for a missing book; raise HTTPException(status_code=404, ...) instead
The function should return a string
The error message should be in a header
questions.explanation: Returning a dict always produces 200, so every client and monitoring tool counts the failure as a success. HTTPException sends a 404 with the detail message.

questions.question: Why should an API never include a stack trace in an error response?
questions.answer: Stack traces reveal file paths, library versions, SQL and code structure that help attackers. Log the trace on the server and return a generic message with a status code.
questions.explanation: Debug pages and verbose errors are a classic source of information disclosure. A request id in the response lets support find the full trace in the logs.

questions.question: How do you make a test use a fake user instead of the real get_current_user dependency?
choices: Delete the dependency from the endpoint during tests
Edit the endpoint to accept a test flag
questions.explanation: dependency_overrides maps the original dependency to a replacement for every endpoint that uses it. Clear it after the test (a fixture can do this) so tests do not leak into each other.

questions.question: Complete the dependency so the session is always closed after the request.
questions.explanation: yield hands the session to the endpoint and pauses; FastAPI resumes the function after the response, so finally runs the close. With return, the finally block would close the session before the endpoint used it.

questions.question: Which are good jobs for a FastAPI dependency? Select all that apply.
choices: Providing a database session per request
Authenticating the caller and returning the current user
Holding the business rules for calculating an invoice total
Loading application settings once and sharing them
questions.explanation: Dependencies supply what endpoints need: resources, identity, parameters, configuration. Business rules belong in plain functions or services that endpoints call, so they stay testable on their own.

questions.question: Two dependencies used by the same endpoint both declare Depends(get_db). During one request, how many times does get_db run?
choices: It raises an error for the duplicate
Once: FastAPI caches a dependency's result within a request
questions.explanation: By default FastAPI reuses a dependency's value within one request, so both see the same session and the same transaction. Depends(get_db, use_cache=False) would force a separate call.

questions.question: Looping over 50 books and printing book.author.name runs 51 SQL queries. What fixes it?
choices: Load authors with the books, for example select(Book).options(selectinload(Book.author))
questions.explanation: Each first access to book.author lazily loads it with its own query. selectinload (or joinedload) fetches all the authors in one extra query up front, turning 51 queries into 2.

questions.question: Put the steps for changing a production database schema with Alembic in order.
items: Generate a migration with alembic revision --autogenerate
Review and edit the generated script
Commit it with the code change
Run alembic upgrade head during deployment
questions.explanation: Autogenerate is a draft, not a guarantee (it can miss renames, for example), so a human reviews it. The migration ships with the code and runs as part of the release.

questions.question: This lookup is vulnerable. What is the problem?
choices: The query should use LIKE instead of =
The f-string puts user input into the SQL text, allowing SQL injection; pass it as a parameter
questions.explanation: A title such as x' OR '1'='1 changes the query's logic. conn.execute("... WHERE title = ?", (title,)) sends the value separately, so it is always treated as data.

questions.question: Apply all pending Alembic migrations to the database.
questions.explanation: head is the newest revision. Deployment pipelines run this before (or as) the new code starts, so the schema matches what the code expects.

questions.question: Which is the right way to store user passwords?
choices: With a slow, salted password hash such as argon2, bcrypt or scrypt
In plain text in a separate table
Encrypted with AES so they can be recovered
questions.explanation: Slow, salted hashes make stolen databases expensive to crack, and the salt defeats precomputed tables. Fast hashes like plain SHA-256 can be guessed billions of times per second, and anything reversible can be reversed by whoever steals the key.

questions.question: Which statements about JWT access tokens are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Anyone holding the token can read its payload, because it is only base64-encoded
The signature stops a client from changing the claims undetected
A JWT can be revoked instantly by deleting it on the server
Short expiry times limit the damage of a stolen token
It is safe to put the user's password in the payload because it is signed
questions.explanation: Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality. Because servers verify JWTs without a lookup, there is nothing to delete; revocation needs short lifetimes, refresh tokens or a deny list.

questions.question: A request arrives with a valid token, but the user's role is not allowed to delete books. Which HTTP status code should the API return?
questions.explanation: 401 means not authenticated (no or bad credentials). This caller is known, just not permitted, so 403 Forbidden.

questions.question: Why compare tokens and password hashes with hmac.compare_digest instead of ==?
questions.answer: == stops at the first different character, so response times leak how much of a guess was right. compare_digest takes the same time regardless, preventing timing attacks.
questions.explanation: Timing differences are tiny but measurable over many requests. Security-sensitive comparisons of secrets should always be constant-time.

questions.question: What does FastAPI's TestClient do when a test calls client.get("/books/1")?
choices: Reads the response from a recorded cassette file
Opens a real network connection to a running server
Runs the request through the app in-process (routing, validation, dependencies) and returns the response
questions.explanation: TestClient talks to the ASGI app directly, so tests exercise the full request handling without starting uvicorn or touching the network.

questions.question: Which checks belong in the test suite for a POST /orders endpoint? Select all that apply.
choices: A valid order returns 201 and the created order in the body
A payload with a negative quantity returns 422
A request without a token returns 401
One user cannot read another user's order
The framework's router matches URLs correctly
questions.explanation: Test your contract and your rules: success, validation, authentication and authorization. The framework's own routing is already tested by its maintainers.
questions.concept: what to test in an API

questions.question: test_admin_only passes when run alone but fails when run after test_member_view. What is the likely cause?
choices: The override set in test_member_view is never removed, so the second test runs with a fake member user
questions.explanation: dependency_overrides is global to the app. Setting it inside a test without restoring it leaks state; do it in a fixture that clears the overrides after the yield, or use monkeypatch-style cleanup.

questions.question: Four requests hit an async def endpoint that calls time.sleep(1) at the same moment, on one worker. Roughly how long until the last response?
questions.explanation: time.sleep blocks the event loop, so the requests are handled one after another. With await asyncio.sleep(1), or a plain def endpoint in the thread pool, they would overlap and finish in about 1 second.

questions.question: Which tasks should go to a task queue with workers rather than run inside the request? Select all that apply.
choices: Sending a batch of 5,000 notification emails
Reading one row by primary key
questions.explanation: Slow or heavy work moves to workers so responses stay fast and the job can be retried. Quick lookups and validation are part of answering the request.

questions.question: What is the trade-off of FastAPI's BackgroundTasks compared with a task queue such as Celery or RQ?
questions.answer: BackgroundTasks is simple and needs no extra infrastructure, but runs in the web process after the response and is lost if the process dies, with no retries. A queue persists jobs and runs them in separate workers with retries and scaling.
questions.explanation: Use BackgroundTasks for small best-effort work. Anything that must happen, takes long, or needs retries belongs on a queue.

questions.question: Which change belongs in production but not on your laptop?
choices: Running several worker processes behind a load balancer that terminates HTTPS
Printing every SQL statement with echo=True
questions.explanation: --reload, echo=True and localhost-only binding are development conveniences. Production runs multiple workers on all interfaces behind a proxy or load balancer that handles TLS.

questions.question: Put the steps of a typical deploy of a new API version in order.
items: CI runs the tests on the merged commit
Build and push the Docker image
Roll out the new containers gradually
Watch health checks, error rates and latency
questions.explanation: Tests gate the build, migrations prepare the schema before new code depends on it, and a gradual rollout with monitoring lets you roll back before every user is affected.

questions.question: Why does the Dockerfile copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying the rest of the code?
choices: pip cannot see the code otherwise
Docker caches that layer, so code-only changes rebuild in seconds instead of reinstalling every package
requirements.txt must be the first file in any image
questions.explanation: Each instruction is a cached layer, rebuilt only when its inputs change. Dependencies change rarely and code changes often, so installing dependencies first keeps rebuilds fast.

questions.question: Start the FastAPI app object app in app/main.py with uvicorn, listening on all interfaces on port 8000, with 4 worker processes.
questions.explanation: app.main:app is module path, colon, variable name. --host 0.0.0.0 accepts connections from outside the container or machine, and --workers starts several processes to use more CPU cores.
